answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 106–43 BC · Roman statesman, orator and philosopher
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Cicero: the line is from the Ninth Philippic (delivered in the Senate in early 43 BC), spoken in honour of the envoy Servius Sulpicius Rufus, who died on a mission to Mark Antony. The Latin is well attested — “Vita enim mortuorum in memoria est posita vivorum.” The English shown is a faithful literal rendering of “est posita” (“is placed / set”), though the standard published translations word it a little differently.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Section 5 (§10), delivered in the Senate, early 43 BC
Vita enim mortuorum in memoria est posita vivorum
English wording shown is a literal rendering; standard translations differ (Yonge; Loeb/Ker 1926; Duncan)

source.excerpt: Reddite igitur, patres conscripti, ei vitam, cui ademistis. Vita enim mortuorum in memoria est posita vivorum. [Restore then, conscript fathers, life to him from whom you have taken it away; for the life of the dead is placed in the memory of the living.]
trail: The Latin original — “Vita enim mortuorum in memoria est posita vivorum” — and its place in Philippic IX are confirmed on Wikiquote ↗, which cites William Duncan’s translation “The life of the dead is in the memory of the living.”
The Loeb text (W.C.A. Ker, 1926) renders the line “the life of the dead is set in the memory of the living” — see the Ninth Philippic on Attalus ↗.

C.D. Yonge’s widely-reprinted public-domain translation gives it as “the life of the dead consists in the recollection cherished of them by the living” (Lexundria ↗) — note that none of these standard versions use the popular word “placed.”
source.excerptNote: Cicero is urging the Senate to vote public honours — a statue and a tomb — for Servius Sulpicius Rufus, an ambassador who died in service. The argument is that remembrance itself confers a kind of immortality.

source.rightsNote: The ancient Latin is public domain. The exact English wording shown — “placed in the memory of the living” — is a popular literal rendering of Cicero’s “est posita” that we could not trace to a specific identifiable published translation; the standard scholarly versions read differently (Yonge: “consists in the recollection cherished of them by the living”; Loeb/W.C.A. Ker, 1926: “set in the memory of the living”). Because the translator and first printing of this precise rendering are unconfirmed, we assert no copyright status for it.

author.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC) was Rome’s greatest orator and a prolific writer on rhetoric, politics and philosophy. After Julius Caesar’s assassination he delivered the Philippics, a series of blistering speeches against Mark Antony — a campaign that ultimately cost him his life when Antony’s men had him killed in 43 BC. Much of what later Europe knew of Greek philosophy came filtered through his Latin.

Yonge: “the life of the dead consists in the recollection cherished of them by the living” (Yonge trans. ↗); the Loeb (W.C.A. Ker, 1926): “the life of the dead is set in the memory of the living” (Attalus ↗).

context.heading: Why it was said
lead: Cicero delivered the Ninth Philippic in the Roman Senate in early 43 BC. The Senate had sent three envoys to negotiate with Mark Antony; one of them, the distinguished jurist Servius Sulpicius Rufus, was already ill and died on the journey. Cicero rose to propose that the state honour him with a bronze statue and a public tomb.

It is in that argument — that a man who gives his life in service should be repaid with lasting remembrance — that Cicero frames memory as a form of immortality: the dead go on living in the minds of those who remember them. The line has since drifted far from its senatorial setting to become a consolation read at funerals and engraved on memorials.
context.pull: Restore life to him from whom you have taken it — for the life of the dead is placed in the memory of the living.
